children.value: This chapter documents the models that use questionnaire (trait / symptom) scores as predictors of behavioural metrics, which is the most direct analysis level for the internalizing and anxiety hypotheses. It is implemented in
symptom_behavior_models.py
and draws its data from the master table described in
Cross-layer Integration: Overview

What this integration layer contributes is proper regression with covariate control, condition moderation, both a participant-level (two-stage) and a trial-level (hierarchical) route, and outcome-appropriate models for the categorical and temporal behavioural targets.
Behavioural targets
The behavioural outcomes fall into three families:
Model-independent summary metrics
, namely defense rate, mean angular error, net entropy, placement speed; one continuous value per participant.
GLMM-derived per-participant scalars
, namely cue-dissociation rate, evidence-dependence slope, the Rule-1 marker (post-transition belief shift). These are the individual-difference measures distilled by the behavioural pipeline (see
Primary GLMMs
Categorical / temporal outcomes
, which include the rule-applier class (modelled by logistic regression) and discovery episode (related to traits by rank correlation, given the small applier subsample)
Two-stage (participant-level) models
For every (trait, target) pair, two participant-level OLS models are fit on standardised variables:

target ~ trait                          [+ covariates]      (main effect)
target ~ trait * condition_L            [+ covariates]      (moderation)
The first asks whether the trait predicts the behavioural metric; the second asks whether that relationship is moderated by instruction depth (a
trait : condition_L

interaction). Covariates (age, sex) are included when present in the merged table. The full trait x target grid of main-effect tests is corrected with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR as an exploratory family; the interaction tests are corrected as a separate family because they answer a different question. Both the main-effect and interaction FDR families are flagged hypothesis-generating.
Hierarchical (trial-level) models
Why both a two-stage and a hierarchical route

The two-stage approach collapses each participant to one summary value and is transparent and robust. The hierarchical approach uses all trials and a participant random intercept, which is more powerful but heavier and, importantly, requires care in interpretation when the predictor of interest varies only
between
participants. The two are offered together so they can be read against each other.
For a small set of headline trial-level outcomes (
angular_error_deg
defense_rate
), the script additionally fits a mixed model with the trait as a between-participant (level-2) predictor:
trial_outcome ~ trait_z + condition_L + (1 | participant)
using
mixedlm
for the Gaussian outcome and
BinomialBayesMixedGLM
(variational Bayes) for the per-trial binary outcome. These fit where feasible and record their fit method and convergence; some are tight at the current N and fall back gracefully.
Interpreting the hierarchical fixed effects

When a between-participant predictor (a trait, constant within participant) is entered into a trial-level mixed model with thousands of trials, the standard error on that predictor can be driven down by trial-level variance that is unrelated to the between-participant contrast, producing implausibly small p-values. In the current run with N = 34, the hierarchical
defense_rate

models returned highly “significant” trait effects (e.g. IU → defense rate, p < 10⁻⁵) that are entirely absent from the two-stage analysis on the same data. Where the two routes disagree this sharply, the
two-stage estimate is the honest readout

of the between-participant relationship, and the hierarchical fixed effect should be treated with suspicion until the random-effect structure has been checked (e.g. confirming the trait coefficient is stable when the model is reduced to a random intercept only). The hierarchical models are retained for the headline outcomes but are not, at present, the basis for any between-participant trait claim.
Categorical and temporal outcomes
Rule-applier class
is reduced to a binary indicator (immediate or late applier = 1) and modelled by logistic regression on each trait, controlling for condition:
rule_applier_is_applier ~ trait_z + condition_L
This asks whether a trait raises or lowers the odds of applying the structural rule, over and above the instruction manipulation. The exploratory family is FDR-corrected.
Discovery episode

(when an applier first reliably applies the rule) is related to traits by Spearman correlation, restricted to the applier subsample. This is the analysis that speaks to the hypothesis that a stronger tendency to find patterns may come with earlier discovery (and may relate to mental-health measures). It is deliberately not FDR-corrected, since at the pilot N the applier subsample is tiny (often well under ten) but might still be insightful to already investigate to eventually control for interactions in future analyses, so this is purely descriptive / hypothesis-generating and is flagged as such, to be revisited at the target N.
Reading the pilot results

At N = 32 the two-stage main effects are uniformly modest and none survive FDR, which is obviously not suprising. However, the value of running this layer now is in establishing the pipeline and the operationalisations, not in the any point estimates.
